exercises.question: What is the purpose of interpreter in TypeScript-like intro to Python for Data?
exercises.answer: interpreter lets you comments — see chapter section 1.2.

exercises.question: Modify the example to keep three decimal places instead of two.
exercises.answer: Format the printed value with the language's precision formatter (e.g. printf/round), then re-run and compare.

exercises.question: When would you avoid comments?
exercises.answer: Avoid it when the task is better served by a simpler, linear approach — momentum matters more than cleverness.

tests.instructions: One assessment per chapter grouping plus a final exam. Every question maps to the section shown in brackets so you can revise precisely.

questions.q: Which concept makes interpreter behave that way? (TypeScript-like intro to Python for Data ch.1)

The worked sample prints "What is your name? Alio
Hello, Alio!". Which statement caused it? (ch.1)
Which concept makes int behave that way? (TypeScript-like intro to Python for Data ch.2)

The worked sample prints "<class 'float'> <class 'int'>
89.97000000000001". Which statement caused it? (ch.2)
Which concept makes if/elif/else behave that way? (TypeScript-like intro to Python for Data ch.3)
The worked sample prints "108.0". Which statement caused it? (ch.3)
Which concept makes def behave that way? (TypeScript-like intro to Python for Data ch.4)
The worked sample prints "10.0". Which statement caused it? (ch.4)
Which concept makes list behave that way? (TypeScript-like intro to Python for Data ch.5)
The worked sample prints "[92]". Which statement caused it? (ch.5)
Which concept makes class behave that way? (TypeScript-like intro to Python for Data ch.6)
The worked sample prints "Python". Which statement caused it? (ch.6)
Which concept makes files behave that way? (TypeScript-like intro to Python for Data ch.7)
The worked sample prints "Missing file". Which statement caused it? (ch.7)
